column1: In control theory, what condition makes a linear time-invariant system 'observable'?
column2: The observability matrix O = [C; CA; CA²; ...; CA^(n-1)] must have full rank n — meaning every internal state mode can be reconstructed from external outputs.

column1: What is the key operational distinction between monitoring and observability?
column2: Monitoring collects predefined signals to answer known questions ('Is error rate above 1%?'). Observability provides rich, correlated signals that let you answer arbitrary, unanticipated questions post hoc without modifying code.

column1: Why does Grafana Loki avoid full-text indexing of log bodies, unlike Elasticsearch?
column2: Because log entropy is dominated by a small set of templates (H(T) is negligible since |T| << |L|); Loki indexes only metadata labels and compresses log bodies, exploiting the fact that most storage cost comes from variable values, not templates.

column1: What is the fundamental tension in log durability vs. latency, and how is it resolved?
column2: A log isn't durable until fsync'd/replicated, but blocking the app thread on that flush degrades latency. This is resolved via asynchronous buffering, which introduces a risk window where in-memory buffered data can be lost on crash.

column1: What three structural invariants define a well-formed distributed trace (as a DAG)?
column2: 1) Single root span with no incoming edges. 2) Acyclicity (no cycles, causality is irreversible). 3) Temporal consistency: a parent span's start/end time must encompass its children's lifetimes.

column1: What is the architectural difference between CHILD_OF and FOLLOWS_FROM span relationships in OpenTelemetry?
column2: CHILD_OF implies the parent is blocked waiting on the child to complete. FOLLOWS_FROM implies the parent initiated the child but doesn't depend on its result (e.g., fire-and-forget async work). Using the wrong one corrupts trace waterfall visualizations.

column1: In signal detection theory applied to alerting, how are Precision and Recall defined, and why do they conflict?
column2: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) (fraction of alerts that are real problems); Recall = TP/(TP+FN) (fraction of real problems that trigger alerts). Lowering the alert threshold raises recall but lowers precision — they trade off against each other.

column1: What are the four invariants of a well-formed, production-ready alert?
column2: 1) Actionability (maps to a runbook). 2) Causality, not correlation (alert on symptoms like latency/errors, not proxies like CPU%). 3) Temporal stability (window suppresses noise but allows timely detection). 4) (implied) ownership to avoid alert fatigue/erosion of on-call trust.

column1: What is the irreducible atom of a metric, formally?
Why is a raw Counter value meaningless in isolation, and what operation makes it aggregation-safe?
column2: A counter only monotonically increases and resets on restart, so raw values carry no rate information. Applying rate(counter[window]) produces per-second increments that are safely summable across replicas: sum(rate(requests_total[5m])).

column1: Why is a Gauge NOT aggregation-safe over time windows?
column2: Because a gauge is a point-in-time measurement (e.g., memory bytes), averaging it over a window (avg(memory_bytes[5m])) yields the window average, not the current value — the correct aggregation function (max/last/avg) depends on semantic intent.

column1: Per the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem applied to metrics scrape intervals, why can't a 10-second scrape interval capture a 100ms latency spike?
column2: To faithfully reconstruct a signal changing at frequency f, you must sample at ≥2f. A 10-second interval is far too coarse to resolve 100ms events — it can only observe their aggregate footprint (e.g., in a histogram bucket), not the individual spike.
